speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make any extended remarks on this bill at this time, other than to say that the object of the minister in bringing in this legislation will not be attained. Perhaps the reason for bringing in this bill was to have legislation which would provide for the whole meat industry such regulations and conditions as would be in the interests of all concerned. Other people than consumers are involved in the quality and distribution of meat in this country. The interests of all these people should be taken into consideration.
The bill says the intention is to inspect meat and meat products entering into interprovincial and international trade. The explanatory note states that where the bill conflicts with the Meat and Canned Foods Act, those sections of the Meat and Canned Foods Act will be revoked. It seems to me that here again we have legislation that is cluttered up with the provisions of another act, and therefore it will not bring satisfactory results to the meat industry. The Meat and Canned Foods Act provides for the inspection of canned meats under sanitary conditions. It appears to me that all the new legislation does is perhaps delete some sections of the Meat and Canned Foods Act and set up a force to carry out the intentions of the new act.
I would ask the minister to give us assurance that there is not going to be a duplication of personnel and services. It seems to me that under the Meat and Canned Foods Act we can have adequate inspection without bringing in this new legislation. It would appear to me that so far as a product entering into international or interprovincial trade is concerned, as long as it is covered by careful inspection from the time it leaves the farmer until it enters the processing field that should be guarantee enough.

In my opinion this new legislation will not deal with some of the problems confronting our meat industry, both from the producer and consumer standpoints. I shall confine my remarks at this time to what I have said, and will have more extended remarks to make when we are dealing with Bill No. 411, to establish national standards for agricultural products and to regulate international and interprovincial trade in agricultural products.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
This was the report of 1934. Here we have a recommendation that a commission be set up to investigate the livestock trade in Canada, but the Liberal government has done nothing about it to date. I think the time is long overdue when some consideration should be given to such commission reports and that, as asked for in this report, a livestock board should be set up.
If such a board were set up with adequate producer, and government consumer representation, I think we could have in Canada a regulatory body by means of which the livestock trade in this country could be handled in the interests of all the people concerned, namely the producers, the people in the processing trades, and also the consumers. The livestock producers do not want anything unfair. They have never asked for high prices out of line with their cost of production. When we have a situation where the livestock producer is at the mercy of the packers I think it is time for the spokesmen

for those people in the house to bring these matters to the attention of the government.
I might say that under the present marketing set-up for our livestock products, the farmer is obliged to send his cattle to the livestock yards at Winnipeg or Toronto, and there he is faced with at least 12 different grades in respect of cattle. We have choice, good, medium, common, cutters and many other grades-12 of them in all-in which his cattle can be placed. With respect to his hogs there is a similar number of grades including, bacon, butcher, light, heavy, light sows and heavy sows.
The producer would feel content, or at least better satisfied, if these grades were carried through to the consumer, but that is not the case. The packers can get together and set the price practically any Monday morning or any day of the week, and also set the quality. There are no government grades. The buyers come in there and compete for the cattle. Perhaps the quotations on one specific day may give a certain price for choice animals, another price for good, another price for medium, and so on down the line. When those cattle come in, if there happens to be a heavy run on the market the buyers can get together and by co-operation force down the price the farmer gets for his livestock. Choice, good and medium cattle may all be listed that day at a certain price, but through the downgrading of those cattle the farmer takes a beating.
The same thing is true with respect to hogs. It is true that hogs are rail graded and government inspected, but there again there is no assurance that while the farmer gets a return on a heavy type hog, the consumer does not pay the same as for a bacon hog. Hence the situation is completely unsatisfactory.
The bill proposed by the minister to set up these national standards for agricultural products does not, in my opinion, solve the problem which confronts us. I am suggesting to the minister and to the government that they seriously consider setting up a national livestock marketing board with producer, consumer and government representation whereby this whole thing may be investigated. We should have competent people on the board in order that for the first time we may have a marketing and processing system in Canada which will be fair to livestock producers.
I might just quote from an article in order to show that at the present time there is dishonest grading with respect to livestock in

this country. This is an excerpt from the Globe and Mail of June 8, 1950. It is fairly old, but the same conditions prevail today. The article reads as follows:
Quelph, June 7-Eastern Canadian housewives are ignorant of beef quality and as a result they are handed whatever their vendor likes to give them, Professor E. Stillwell of Ontario Agricultural College told a gathering of 500 Shorthorn breeders and their families at a demonstration of beef grading at the college here today.
Producing 12 cuts of beef, he told his audience that they were purchased in various parts of Ontario as choice prime cuts, at prices ranging from 65 to 79 cents per pound, in the past few days. Not one cut could be called choice prime beef.
In no instance was any of the team of purchasers, sent out under the auspices of Professor Knox, head of O.A.C. animal husbandry department, and the Ontario Shorthorn association directors, able to purchase red or blue ribbon beef, first and second grades respectively. All the beef purchased was of commercial quality, some of it very poor.
Hence you can see that under the present system of grading and assembling meat, in the retail end of it our consumers too are getting fleeced, one might say. I therefore strongly urge that this house and the government consider setting up a national livestock marketing board on which we shall have, as I say, producer representation, consumer representation and also government officials, who will co-operate in order to give all the people concerned the best kind of marketing set-up with respect to livestock products.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make just a few brief comments on this bill, which to me appears a sensible piece of legislation, as far as it goes, in consolidating, as it does, five other acts. It provides for what appears to be strict enforcement of national standards for farm products. I am quite sure that farmers welcome national standards. I am quite sure the great majority of farmers want to produce commodities of high standard and up to certain grades. However, I think the farmer also is entitled to see that national standards are applied to many of the things he purchases.
Before dealing with that matter for a moment or two, I want to mention the fact that we have fairly strict grading laws with regard to vegetables, meats, dairy products, poultry and fruit. The hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) has mentioned something in connection with meat. I would not be as competent as some of the members of this group or other members of the house to judge a prime cut. However, I know something about fruit because I have packed a good many thousand boxes of apples in my lifetime. Over a period of two or three years I packed apples for 10 cents a box, net return, and nearly starved to death.
Agricultural Products
I want to bring to the attention of the minister the argument that while it is quite all right to enforce national standards on the farmer, under which he must produce apples to a certain standard and grade, poultry to a standard and grade and eggs to a standard and grade, in fairness that requirement must be carried through and the government must see that wholesalers and retailers market these products according to the grades marked by the producer. I have visited stores in Calgary, in Winnipeg and in Ottawa, and repeatedly I have found apples in retailers' windows raised above the grade which the farmer received when he sold them to the packing house in question or to the farm organization. I think there must be stricter enforcement of the act, not only so far as the farmer is concerned-for on the whole he produces the material according to the standard required-but in the distribution of the farmer's product grades are often changed.
I mentioned that I think the farmers are entitled to more protection with respect to commodities they buy from other producers and manufacturers. What protection has the farmer in this country when he is buying fencing wire? I think it is only as the result of some excellent work on the part of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that there has been some improvement in the tensile strength of fencing wire in recent years. What protection has he when he buys roofing? You can get five or six different prices for certain types of roofing, and I have heard from people in the national research council, who understand these things, that you are paying different prices for much the same thing. What about paints? Paints are one of the biggest rackets we have in this country, and the price range is very great. You are not certain when you pay the higher price that you are getting a quality that much better.
I believe these are things that need investigation. The government should apply the same standards, the same enforcement, to the things the farmers buy. I particularly want to mention mill feeds. I was at a farmers' meeting just prior to coming to Ottawa and was shown some samples from a sack of mill feed, crushed oats as a matter of fact, from some milling company on the prairie. It was a positive disgrace. The sample was full of wild oats and other weeds, and was far below standard. I believe there is a great deal more that has to be done in this regard, and action should not be taken merely with respect to those commodities the farmers produce.

Agricultural Products
As I said before, I believe the bill is necessary, and it tidies up the legislation. When the minister replies I should like him to inform the house whether the farmers' organizations were consulted about this legislation. Have they been asked for any suggestions or recommendations? This is a very important piece of legislation so far as the marketing of farm products is concerned. I feel the major agricultural organizations should have been informed of the government's intention and asked for any suggestions or advice they wished to offer.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I again say that the legislation seems to be sound and necessary, but I do hope the government enforces similar national standards on the products the farmers and other consumers have to buy.

Probably I should make a few remarks in reply to what has been said by different hon. members. There was some discussion on third reading of the meat products bill which really relates to this bill, and probably I should make a remark or two with regard to that.
The meat inspection bill, which had its third reading a little while ago, does not provide for the employment of any immediate additional staff to those we have now and no change from the present act as to the future. The staff provided for in present legislation will take care of our activities in connection with both these measures. Then there was a suggestion the other evening which left the impression that the meat inspection act might have been dealing with some of the matters with which the bill now before us deals. The meat inspection act does not cover grading. The meat inspection act deals only with health inspection and sanitation, and therefore does not provide for grading in the sense this bill does. I just wanted to make those remarks as they may have some bearing on the discussion that may take place in committee.
The purpose of the new bill is to provide acceptable uniform authorities for establishing grade standards, and to perform the grading and inspection of all agricultural products previously covered by five separate acts administered by the Department of Agriculture. The new general bill is patterned after the Canada Dairy Products Act, enacted in 1951, which has proven satisfactory for dairy products. It provides authority for establishing substantially the same regulations
[Mr. Herridee.)

as now exist, but is considered to have the purposes and intentions more clearly defined and restricted to the established and accepted field of federal jurisdiction specifically related to the grading and quality standards of our agricultural products.
In dealing with the other bill the other day I believe I said some question has been raised in the courts as to whether some of these measures are intra vires. That was one of the reasons it was thought wise to introduce this bill now. The bill will provide, as in the past, for the actual grading of certain products by federal graders, and for others the application of established grades and standards by the trade with subsequent checking of the applied standards by federal inspectors, and detention until they are made to comply with the official standards. The provisions of the bill will apply where the products enter into interprovincial or export trade, or where as the result of legislation on the part of the provinces or action on the part of the individual the product bears a grade name established pursuant to this act.
The grading of a product moving intra-provincially will, therefore, depend upon action by the provinces. In addition to defining standards and carrying out grade inspection operations the bill provides, as in the past, for a regulatory service with respect to such matters of packaging, marking and shipping products and the operation of grading establishments dealing in products exported from or imported into a province.
These remarks are related to what was said a few moments ago by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough), who was suggesting that certain things might be done which were proposed back in 1934. As a matter of fact the marketing act which was drafted as a result of the committee's report in 1934 went to the courts and was declared ultra vires. No effort has been made since then to pass similar legislation.
The reason for that is that the provinces deal with these matters. The questions which were raised a few moments ago concerning the price of meat in Toronto and the price of meat in Winnipeg, as between retailer and consumer, are matters which should be dealt with provincially. If we attempted to put in this particular legislation anything relating to that matter it would be declared ultra vires, just as the other legislation was. In other words only a small percentage of the meat products produced in a province are consumed outside of that province. Most of the meat products that are produced in a province are consumed in that province.

This is largely true of the older and more industrialized provinces, such as Ontario and Quebec. They consume more of practically all these farm products than they produce, but that does not mean there is no trade as between the provinces in these products.
Perhaps the greatest exporters of surplus meat products are the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. They do produce large quantities of meat, some of which goes to Ontario and some to British Columbia. Much of the Alberta meat goes to British Columbia, and some of it goes down along the western coast. On the other hand, much of what is produced in Saskatchewan finds its way to Winnipeg, and some of it finds its way to Toronto and Montreal. In so far as these products are concerned, of course, we have something to say about them. In so far as practically all the meat products produced in Ontario are concerned, which are not shipped to the United States or not shipped to Montreal to be consumed there, they are consumed within Ontario.
I should like to say a word in reply to the hon. member for Moose Mountain by stating that there are only two provinces in Canada that have paid very much attention to the matter of marketing boards. One of them is British Columbia, where they have a very complete system of control over the marketing of their fruit and other products. Then in Ontario there are 18 different boards handling 18 different farm products, one of which is hogs. But so far as I know we have no boards in the province from which my hon. friend comes, and they keep suggesting that we ought to have a federal department do their work.
Well, the experience has been that it is difficult to have a federal board to do the work which it has been suggested should be done. Any attempts that have been made to do it have resulted in difficulty for those passing the legislation. But amendments are being asked by Ontario, which has set up many of these boards, and legislation is being asked by some who are active in British Columbia. Also legislation is being asked by some of the other provinces which we propose to bring down, and which will amend the legislation which does have some control over the relationship between the selling of the product within the province and the selling of it under similar terms outside the province.
Just to answer the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge), it is our intention to bring some legislation before the house along the lines of the representations which have been made. Representations have been made by farm organizations and also by representatives of the governments I have mentioned. They have
Agricultural Products
come here asking for legislation, and legislation is under consideration to make it possible for the legislation they have in the province to be more effective than it could be without the amendments. I have suggested on a number of occasions to those in my own province and to those in other provinces similarly situated, that the method being followed in Ontario and British Columbia, and to a limited extent in some of the other provinces, could be used more extensively in the provinces where very little use has been made of it.
That is the question which has been investigated by a committee set up in Saskatchewan and, in a little different form, by a committee set up recently in Manitoba to examine into the possibility of operating boards controlled by the farmers themselves in order to market these products. But when we come to deal with a product produced in Ontario and placed on the market in Toronto, where it is sold to someone living in that city; when we are asked to do something about it here-well, I am afraid the experience and judgment of the past have indicated that this can be done only by the people of Ontario through their own legislature. They have very effective ways of dealing with it and, I must say, in some directions have done more in an effort to grapple with the problem than has been done in some other provinces. This bill is intended only to deal with exports either from one province to another or from this country to some other country.

That of course has been a matter of discussion for many years. It was under discussion long before I came here, and it has been under discussion now for 20 years since I have been here. The solution was found before I had anything to do with it, or before many of the members of this house had much to do with it. The statements I was making a few moments ago were based upon my knowledge of the legal position, and my knowledge may not be as good as that of the hon. member who has just spoken in regard to that side of it. But in order to get the results which he and others desire, the arrangement was made a long time ago that if there is to be a standard at all across Canada, it must be a standard set up by the federal government.
For many years there was some dispute as to whether the standards set up for dairy products were to apply everywhere. My memory of it is that the last province which came under the arrangement was Manitoba. They were consuming practically all of their butter in Winnipeg and other places of that

kind, and they did not wish to conform to the federal standard. Eventually they did so, and when that happened they did just what others had been doing in a broad sense all across Canada for some years. They accepted the standards which had been set up here as the proper standards.
We appointed inspectors to establish those grades for butter, as we had for all other products that were going to be traded inter-provincially or internationally. Then the provincial inspectors inspected the product that was to be sold within the province itself. But to just leave it that way you would have to know all the time what product was to go into interprovincial trade and what was to be sold within the province. In order to overcome the impossibility of knowing that, when an inspector is inspecting a product that eventually goes out of the province, he is a federal inspector. Whenever one of our inspectors inspects a product which is sold within the province, he is acting as a provincial inspector.
That arrangement, which was entered into years ago, has been carried out consistently over the years, in order to make it legally possible to have all the products so inspected that are to be sold either internally or shipped out and sold outside. The legal position, though, is that which I stated a few moments ago.

I quarrel with the discrepancies that sometimes prevail between what the packers pay for meat and what we as dealers pay for it. There is room for argument there, but not in this ease. Agricultural Products
have to be fair enough to realize. For instance, if you come into my store and I try to sell you a commercial grade by telling you it is red brand; I am just deliberately lying. There is no retail merchant who does not know the difference. If they resort to skulduggery and try to flim-flam the public, one dose of that should be enough for anybody. I do not believe they do that as a general practice. I have seen in many big stores and in my own store, people who want the red brand because they enjoy the excess fat, but I have seen other people who do not want that. If I offer them red brand they complain because of the excess fat. So I have to have in my own shop two grades in order to satisfy the wishes of the customers.
I will agree that this is a common practice. I have seen it here in Ottawa, and I have seen it out in the west, so I suppose it is common across the board to find a certain amount of misrepresentation over the counter so far as the true grade of the beef is concerned. But I think that is beside the point. That is something that could be dealt with apart from grading. It does not necessarily mean that the grade has been tampered with. If the animal is bought as a commercial and cut up and sold as a red brand over the counter, it is not the fault of the initial grading. I believe the grades are honest, and I believe they are uniform.
I would ask those who can do something about it to have a look at these practices whereby commercial is offered under the guise of blue or red brand. I have seen that happen so far as pork is concerned. I have seen it happen with heavy loins that came from No. 1 sows and heavy hogs. Of course we as retailers have to pay the same price. But that is getting into a different grade again. True enough these indiscretions do occur, but you differentiate between a C and a select hog to ensure that you get a square deal over the counter. As I said, the excess fat is trimmed off and that brings it down to the same basis of quality, whether it is a C or a select hog.
As far as lamb is concerned, you have the same grades there. You have lambs and yearling lambs, as they are sometimes called, and you have mutton. If you go into a butcher shop and they try to sell you a half leg of mutton at the level of lamb, that is not the fault of the grades. The grade in the first place was honest. If somebody tries to introduce a little skulduggery over the counter, that is not the fault of the initial grading. People who are getting an unfair deal should look around for a dependable butcher. Government grading has nothing to do with it. Government grading is not the culprit at all
[Mr. Yuill.J

in this case. If they get commercial beef and wrap it up and put it on the counter under the guise of red beef, it is not the fault of the original grader; it is the fault of the man who is selling it to you over the counter.
The sooner we realize what is involved there the better, instead of jumping to conclusions and feeling sorry for ourselves if we market commercial and expect to get red beef grade. The producer must realize that he must first of all get a higher standard of animal, and then see to it that he finishes it properly before he puts it on the market. Then he will have no worries.

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
As far as the act in general is concerned, it has been in effect now since 1935 and represents one of the most effective acts ever placed on the statute books of our country with reference to the restoration of lands and the preservation of moisture. However, today we find ourselves in a position where getting moisture on to the lands is no more important, having regard to the cycle through which we are passing, than getting it off. This act in its present form, with few amendments, has been in effect since 1935. It represents a monument to the vision of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and the Hon. Robert Weir who conceived it and brought it into being. Through their concept tremendous improvements have taken place in our economic position in the western provinces.

In 1952 the act made the concession, if I may put it that way, that projects under $10,000 might be undertaken without the approval of the governor in council. If that was done in 1952, I can see no reason why in 1955 we should increase it by 50 per cent. When we look at the statistical reports of recent days this is what we find. For example, I hold in my hand the Canadian Statistical Review of April, 1955. I find that neither retail nor


wholesale prices have increased by 50 per cent. In fact, in relation to wholesale prices, we find that they are down a little and retail prices are up only slightly. For the life of me I cannot see any reason why we should grant this additional power to the minister.
There is a general feeling among many people in western Canada and in the prairie provinces that there are too many political appointments under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, although it does have many good people in it. It is becoming more and more a political machine directed by the Minister of Agriculture.
When I look at the long list of over 1,400 employees in this report, which was asked for by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), and some 500 under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, I find, as has already been stated, certain appointments made that do not command the respect of this parliament or, I believe, of the country generally.
In asking for this power the minister is asking something from the house that the house should not grant in the circumstances under which this act has been administered. I want to say immediately that since the act was placed on the statute books of this country in 1934 much good has come of it. As a matter of fact, I believe we have had no act as beneficial to the prairie provinces as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; and indeed, as far as it goes, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act placed on the statute books subsequently has also been of substantial benefit to our western agricultural population.
I am joining in the protest against granting this additional power to the minister, not because I wish to deny to him and to the administration the same rights as we have granted to some of the other administrative bodies under the government. I am doing it, as the hon. member for Prince Albert did it, because I feel that somehow or other we have to make as effective a protest as we can against the manner in which a few of the employees of this organization have been appointed, and against the manner in which they are carrying out their activities in the prairie provinces. That is the reason for the opposition which I am voicing to the increase of power given to the minister at this time.
I want the house to understand, Mr. Speaker, that it is not because we wish in any way to hamper the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Indeed, I should like to see it extended and more work undertaken under it. We are asking today that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act shall have some additional money and power to assist in the grave situation which has resulted

from flooding in the prairie provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Therefore, let it not be said that in opposing this particular bill we are in any way endeavouring to hamper the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. What we are doing is endeavouring to make the only effective protest we can make in this house. The only effective protest we can ever make is to refuse to grant money to the government or to a government department. Because of the political activities of some of the persons employed under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, because of some of the appointments which I think not only were unwarranted but were a reflection on this parliament of Canada, I intend to vote against this particular bill.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to oppose this bill for the reasons already outlined, namely, that it gives the minister the power to spend larger amounts of money without having to obtain the approval of the governor in council. In view of the information which has been placed on the record this afternoon by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), I think hon. members would be justified in voting against an approval to spend money without the approval of the governor in council.
I wish to direct my remarks particularly to clause 2 of the bill which repeals sections 10 and 11 of the act. Section 10 of the act reads:
The minister may, for the purposes of this act, and with the approval of the governor in council, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire, or sell, lease or otherwise dispose of, any lands or premises that may be required for or included in any project or scheme, upon such terms or conditions as he may deem desirable.
With that section removed from the act there will no longer be vested in the minister power, in this instance with the approval of the governor in council, to purchase, lease or otherwise acquire, or sell, lease or otherwise dispose of, any lands or premises that may be required for or included in any project. The whole life of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in the past depended upon the ability of the minister to acquire, with the approval of the governor in council in this instance, or lease lands for the purposes of the act. At the present time there is under lease in connection with prairie farm rehabilitation over 1,600,000 acres of pasture land. With this section deleted from the act I am wondering what will be left for prairie farm rehabilitation to undertake. Does it mean that there will be an end to further acquisition of land for pasture purposes? Does it mean that if the governor in council should decide to undertake the South Saskatchewan dam they will not have power under this act to lease property and therefore no power to acquire control of the site on which the dam would be erected?


I am not a lawyer and therefore I am not professing to give an answer to the question I am raising. If power exists for this specific purpose under some other act, then why should this provision have been in the act since 1939? Unless the minister can point out to me a provision in the Financial Administration Act, which would be a substitute for section 10, I cannot see how he is going to be able to carry on the very important functions of prairie farm rehabilitation which depend upon the leasing of land.
Section 11 of the act, which is also to be deleted, reads:
(1)	The minister may, for the purposes of this act, purchase or rent whatever machinery or equipment may be required in connection with the development, construction or operation of any project or scheme, but the purchase of any single unit of machinery or equipment of a value greater than five thousand dollars requires the approval of the governor in council.
(2)	Notwithstanding the provisions of any other act or law, the minister may sell any single unit of such machinery or equipment upon such terms as he may deem advisable and the proceeds thereof shall be paid to the receiver general, but the sale of any such unit, if its initial cost exceeded five hundred dollars, requires the approval of the governor in council.
I direct the attention of the house more particularly to subsection 1 of section 11 of the act which gives the minister the power to acquire machinery worth more than five thousand with the approval of the governor in council. If we are to delete section 10 and section 11, my question is this: Where does the power remain for the government to undertake the very functions of prairie farm rehabilitation which we all think are so important? In other words, if these sections are removed, does that spell the end of pasture leases in the future? Does that spell the end of the acquiring of machinery by the department? Does that mean that for all practical purposes prairie farm rehabilitation has been brought to an end and that the public of Canada in the future will not be able to expect the government to lease land or to purchase equipment? As I say, I hope my fears are groundless. I would certainly like an answer to the question I have proposed, because unless there are very definitely in the Financial Administration Act or some other act all of the necessary powers to replace sections 10 and 11, then this act, which has been a very good act, will for all practical purposes have been destroyed.

were to take the matter up from there and go on and spend money in the way they had been taught by the government of Canada that it should be spent in order to rehabilitate that area. When we came in we decided that was not a big enough way, that there was not sufficient vision in the minds of those who set up that legislation to take care of the problem. The question I was asked across the floor of the house by the then leader of the opposition, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, was the question as to how long we thought it would take to deal with this question. I said it would take at least 20 years and that it would require all the money that we could get from parliament during that 20 years time. The 20 years are now up.
I can understand the question coming from the hon. member for Assiniboia as to whether that is the intention in what is being done now. There was no such intention when this amendment was made to this act. It had nothing of that kind in mind whatsoever. 9. (1) The minister may, (a) subject to section 4,-

-undertake the development, construction, promotion, operation and maintenance of any project or scheme under or by virtue of this act, or enter into agreements with any province, municipality or person with respect thereto:
And then (b):
(b) pay all necessary administrative expenses incurred under the act and all necessary travelling and living expenses incurred by officials or employees in performance of their duty.
If we had been amending that part of the section perhaps my hon. friend would have been quite right to have said something about the officials that were being appointed. But we are not amending that section. Then as to power:
(2) no single project or scheme under this section involving an expenditure in excess of ten thousand dollars in any fiscal year shall be undertaken without the consent of the governor in council.
Now, the reason the words "governor in council" were put in at that time was the reason I gave a few moments ago. There are times when you can get to council more readily than you can wait for the matter to pass through the treasury board. So, at that time we did say that this could be done by simply taking it to council. All we are saying in this bill is that the amount of $10,000 is to be increased to $15,000 to conform to the Financial Administration Act
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which was passed in 1952, I believe, and which made it $15,000 instead of $10,000. Then, we are suggesting again that it go, as every other vote of the kind does, to the treasury board before it goes to council; that is the amendment which is made.
This amendment does not increase the powers of the minister or the powers of the minister plus council, because it was simply a matter of taking it to council in the days when it was decided we wanted to have this thing done rather than have to take the regular course through the treasury board. Now, this amendment sends it back through treasury board as is the procedure in connection with all other departmental affairs and it takes the same course as similar votes do.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 410, to amend the Customs Act.

speechtext: I presume the minister is going to make a statement.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to meet the convenience of the house at this time I shall proceed with the second reading of this Bill 410, to amend the Customs Act. I am sorry that there has been a misunderstanding and perhaps I am somewhat to blame for that. It was not brought to my attention until this morning that we intended to proceed with this bill. During the years I have been in this house it has been customary to have the top officials of the department here, and especially when we go into the committee stage. I quite understand that at this point discussion should deal with the principle of the bill.
This is a simple bill and the essential purpose of it is to clarify and bring up to date certain sections of the Customs Act. Under the present law vehicles are required to report to customs when conveying dutiable goods. As the house is aware, the Department of National Revenue customs and excise division is now charged with the administration of other regulations, such as those involving the health of animals, insect infestations, diseases of plants, and so on. In addition, the departments of immigration and health are also concerned that everyone crossing the border should report. I believe that is normal procedure.
The only difference under this amendment is that, whereas only a person crossing the
Customs Act
border with dutiable goods had to report, now all persons who cross the border have to report to the nearest customs official. He may report there for matters having to do with immigration because immigration officials at border points are usually in the same offices as the customs officials. It may be that such persons would be bringing animals across the border, and under certain regulations which we administer those animals have to be examined and passed. The same situation holds true in connection with certain health regulations.
Under another section of the bill we propose also to amend the valuation sections in order to clarify and confirm our present principles of valuation. It is proposed to limit the period for appeals against the original appraisal.
A third section has to do with the powers of the tariff board. The tariff board will be empowered to hear appeals from departmental rulings affecting export as well as domestic drawbacks. This particular provision has been introduced in order to give the appellant what might be called a fairer chance with reference to matters which he might want to bring to the attention of the board, over and above the customs officials. At the present time, if goods are diverted from the use for which entry was gained at a lesser rate of duty, we can only make a demand for the proper duty from the person found in possession of the goods. It seems desirable to hold the original importer responsible in cases of this kind. Very often we have found that an importer will bring into the country goods on which duty has been paid and then it appears that the valuation of the goods has been changed. In the meantime, he has disposed of the goods to some person and we can only hold that second or third person responsible for the duty. We feel it would be better administration to hold the original importer responsible.
At the present time a lien holder has only 30 days from the date of seizure to apply for a judicial order declaring his interest in the goods or vehicle so seized. It is proposed to extend this time to 60 days. We believe that is a right which should be given to the lien holder, so the period for this declaration will be extended from 30 days to 60 days.
I do not know that there are many other principles involved in the bill that we are considering. What has struck me about the explanations my officials have given with reference to the valuation for duty purposes is that they are based mostly on the value in the country of export under comparable conditions. Very often present trade practices make it impossible to find comparable con-

Customs Act
ditions in the country of export. For instance, let me give you an example without mentioning any names at all. A company doing business in Canada may have their manufacturing plant in the United States, and may take the full output of that particular factory. The factory does not sell to other people in the United States. In that instance, there are not comparable conditions of sale. We feel that the departmental appraisers should have the authority to appraise those goods and apply the rates of duty that are applicable. That is just one of the instances.
I feel that the most important section in the bill is section 35 which has to do with the valuation for duty purposes. Hon. members will recall that a year or two ago we made an amendment to the Customs Act when the matter of dumping duty was brought up. Since that time we have had about 20 appraisers appointed in the different countries. By reason of having these appraisers, we have been able to get better valuations of the goods exported to this country. We have one appraiser in Japan, one in Poland and one in Czechoslovakia. Recently Czechoslovakia was anxious to export goods to Canada. We thought we could not accept their valuation unless an official of our department had access to their cost sheets and to their invoices which they sent out. They have agreed to that and we now have an appraiser in Czechoslovakia. I believe there are about 15 such appraisers in the United States.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: And none in the United Kingdom?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Oh yes, we have had them there. These appraisers I mentioned are in addition to the ones we had a year or two ago when the Customs Act was amended. We have them, of course, in the countries with whom we are trading all the time. We have officials in the United Kingdom, in France and these different countries with whom we have agreements, countries that are extensive exporters to Canada.
As a result of having appraisers in the United States we have been able to establish certain duties. Hon. members will recall that in the debate that took place when the act was amended it was held by some that there was a lot of dumping into this country and there was what was called depressed and end-of-the-line selling. In order to cure that, we had our appraisers take valuations. The manufacturers concerned have given them the freest access to the information. We have had them take valuation of the lines of goods that were coming into this country about which complaints were received, principally textiles. I think perhaps the complaints were the result of the depression of

the textile business in Canada, which I might point out was world-wide and obtained in many other places. It was because of these complaints that our efforts were put forth in connection with textiles, frigidaires and certain electrical goods. As a result of that, where there was what was called depressed selling and end-of-the-line selling we went back over these invoices and took the prices at which the majority of the goods were sold. We had the right to go back over the average prices for a period of six or nine months, or a year-I am not sure of the exact time at the moment.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Six months.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, I believe that is right- six months. Had I the data here I could show thousands upon thousands of invoices, the information from which enabled us- and we did-to put on a price on what might be called end-of-the-line of fire sale or distress goods. We found that the prices at which those goods were entered into Canada were equal to or above the prices charged in the country of export in the days of their earlier and larger sales.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
I am told by my officials that it does. When we come to that section hon. members will see a number of alternative methods by which we get at the valuation. However, we will discuss them in more detail when we get to them.
If we keep in mind the fact that these are values for duty purposes, then we will have a clearer understanding of why you cannot lay down in one rule or one paragraph what shall be the value for duty. Because there are circumstances affecting the situation that do not apply to all types of goods. My opinion, after studying the matter as carefully as I can, is that you cannot have one yardstick which will meet all conditions. And if the first yardstick is not right you have to use another one, and perhaps another one, until you get what you think is a fair market value in the country of export.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a bill of this kind which lumps together a number of amendments to an existing statute, many of which amendments are not related to one another, it is not altogether easy to discern or isolate the principle of the bill. In a bill of this kind there are about as many principles as there are clauses.
However, after hearing the statement made by the minister I suppose the first question arising in the minds of hon. members would

be this: Why, in view of the indicated importance of the matters the bill contains, has it been delayed to this date? We have reached the late stages, we understand, of this session, and we are dealing with a bill which concerns matters all of which have been in existence for some considerable time. There was no mention of the bill in the speech from the throne. Its timing, to say the least, strikes one as being interesting.
There have been those of us in the house who have throughout this session been drawing to the attention of the government, as we did in preceding sessions, the fact that Canadian workmen have been losing their jobs as a result of the dumping in this country of goods that were being grossly undervalued for duty purposes, thereby creating a situation in which Canadian workmen were being called upon to compete against the prices of imported goods on an altogether unfair and unrealistic basis.
Now, no new situation has suddenly arisen in recent days to account for the introduction of this bill at the present time. It is a very important matter, Mr. Speaker. The only conclusion one can reach from the timing of the bill is that the government has been compelled at last to move, even at a limited pace, in the direction of meeting an existing threat.
It is not my purpose to attempt a detailed review of what the bill purports to do. There will be opportunity of course to do that in greater detail at the committee stage of the bill. But, sir, the minister has reviewed sections and has singled out one in particular. I am sure there will be no quarrel in any part of the house with those provisions of the bill which enlarge the right given to persons under the bill to seek relief from seizure or to seek to assert their right in regard to appraisals that are made. So far as the enlargement of the time or the clarification of the rights of appeal are concerned, of course the legislation will be approved.
But, sir, the minister had singled out as the most important provision in the bill the one relating to the amendment of section 85 of the act, pertaining to valuation for duty purposes. This provision will recall to the minds of members the rather stirring debates held in this chamber in December of 1953, at which time subsection 6 was added to section 35 of the Customs Act. That is the provision to which the minister has referred, which gave rise to a new power on the part of the minister to set a special value for customs purposes of goods that were to be brought in on an end-of-line or end-of-season basis.
Hon. members will not need to be reminded that in the course of the debate on that
Customs Act
measure, the famous Bill No. 29, we in this part of the house said that the measure was inadequate for the purposes the government had stated. The result of some days' discussion was to make it abundantly clear it is almost impossible to discuss a subject pertaining to trade or the strengthening of anti-dumping provisions of our existing legislation, even when the bill is introduced by the government, without many hon. members in other parts of the house attempting to bring in some old shibboleths and some old and very base and unwarranted accusations in regard to the position of parties on the subject of trade restrictions.
Sir, let me remind the house that it was the government that then asked the house to strengthen its hands and give it new powers to set special arbitrary valuations on goods imported into Canada. That power was sought by the government for the purpose of dealing with an existing dumping threat. Let us look back to the words of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) that he used in introducing the bill on December 7, 1953, when, as reported at page 673 of Hansard, he said, referring to section 35:
It has been found in practice that the section as it is now worded has not been fully adequate to deal with certain practices which in fact constitute a special kind of dumping.
And later, at page 674, he said:
The importation of such goods into Canada at abnormally low prices may cause injury to Canadian industry which is not in any real sense related to its relative efficiency or productivity. The government believes that this situation needs to be corrected, and to this end is proposing an amendment to the Customs Act.
That amendment, Mr. Speaker, added this new provision, to which I have made reference, to section 35 of the Customs Act. But let it be clearly remembered, sir, that the purpose of this addition to section 35 of the Customs Act was to give the government additional powers to grapple with the problems of dumping of foreign goods in Canada, and particularly United States goods, as we were told at an early stage of the discussion, under conditions that Canadian workmen could not fairly be called upon to meet.
We said that the measure was not adequate for the purpose that the government stated it had in mind. We have waited, sir, for a year and a half for our vindication, and we see our vindication here in this chamber tonight, because the government is back asking the house to replace section 35 with a very different kind of section, a provision that is intended again to strengthen the hands of the government to deal with the problem of dumping as well as the problem of setting

Customs Act
valuations on goods that do not come strictly within the scope of the dumping definition, but are required to have special values set upon them for duty purposes. Yes, the government is coming back to eke out what was left lacking in December, 1953.
Just as we told them at that time, their provisions were inadequate for the purpose that they stated was necessary and to meet the need that was clearly known to the house at that time, and now they come back and ask the house to strengthen their hands to meet these problems. These are the threats to Canadian workmen; these are the threats to employment in Canada. We have seen what these threats have done in the field of textiles, in the field of electric goods and in others, and now the government is back. A year and a half have gone. Many a job no doubt has been lost in the meantime. Now the government, after prodding from the opposition, has asked to add what was left lacking in the face of our warnings in December, 1953.
Well, sir, there will be fuller opportunity to discuss the type of amendment that is now put before the house in this bill when we come to the detailed review in committee stage. But, sir, I hope that hon. members in this house who sought in December, 1953, to picture Her Majesty's loyal opposition as raising the old tariff cry will find in this measure tonight directed at them a rebuke coming from the government, because the government is saying to the house now and saying to its own supporters in this house that it needs more powers to grapple with dumping in Canada and to meet what is lacking today in the government's powers to establish special and arbitrary values for duty purposes.
Now, sir, one would like to know just why the government has waited so long, why the government had to be prodded and pushed into taking measures of this kind. Sir, the minister talks about the difficulties in relation to comparable conditions and a definition of what are comparable conditions. Sir, all these difficulties have existed for years. These are not new expressions in our legislation, and they certainly are not new expressions within the last year and a half. These are expressions that have been embedded in this section for years. Why then does the government suddenly discover now that there are difficulties in determining and defining comparable conditions?
Sir, I think the house will have some questions for which it will need an answer at the hands of the government. Here are some that occur to me. Is there dumping 
in Canada today? Sir, if there is no dumping in Canada today, or if the provisions of our customs legislation are adequate today in the matter of empowering the government to establish special values for duty purposes, then why is this legislation introduced? No; there can be only one conclusion, sir, namely, that the legislation is inadequate and it has been inadequate to prevent dumping, and that dumping is going on today, as we have told this house this long time past.
Then, sir, is that dumping going on today? By whom is it being done? From what countries are the goods being dumped into Canada? How long has this dumping been going on? How long have Canadian workmen been left at the mercy of inadequate legislation in respect of dumping, inadequate legislation in respect of the empowering of the government to establish special values for duty purposes? In what commodities is this dumping going on? How many Canadian workmen have lost their jobs as the result of this dumping, and why, sir, has the government delayed this long to ask the house to give it strengthened powers to grapple with the threats to the livelihood of Canadian workmen?
I asked the minister a question: is this legislation in keeping with the provisions of GATT? The minister answered in the affirmative. It is evident that the opinion of the Department of Justice is that the house is competent to pass this legislation within the provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Sir, that recalls the changes made in this legislation in 1948. It will be remembered that in the legislation as it had existed up to that time there was provision in subsection 3 of section 35 that where neither the fair market value nor the equivalent of such value could be ascertained, the value for duty purposes should be determined to be not less than the actual cost of production of similar goods at the date of the shipment to Canada, plus a reasonable addition for administration, selling cost and profit. The Department of Justice was called upon to give an opinion, after the provisions of GATT came into effect, and they said that that provision in the Customs Act would have to give way in the face of article VI of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Article VI provided in part as follows:
No anti-dumping shall be levied on any product of the territory of any contracting party imported into the territory of any other contracting party in excess of an amount equal to the margin of dumping under which such product is being imported. For the purpose of this article, the margin of dumping shall be understood to mean the amount by which the price of the product exported from one country to another

(a)	is less than the comparable price, in the ordinary course of trade, for the like product when destined for consumption in the exporting country; or
(b)	in the absence of such domestic price, is less than either
(i)	the highest comparable price for the like product for export to any third country in the ordinary course of trade, or
(ii)	the cost of production of the product in the country of origin plus a reasonable addition for selling cost and profit.
Apparently, it was the view of the law officers of the crown that section 35, as it then read, offended those provisions of article VI of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Then in 1948 the government asked the house to amend section 35 so that it might conform with the provisions of GATT. The house did write that amendment into section 35, and from that point on there was provision that only if:
neither the fair market value nor the equivalent of such value can be ascertained, the value for duty shall be the actual cost of production of similar goods at date of shipment to Canada, plus a reasonable addition for administration, selling cost and profit.
In the administration that has been given to that provision since, it has been taken as fundamental that the provisions cannot be applied in any case whatever unless it is impossible to determine the fair market value or the equivalent of such value in the country from which the goods are shipped.
We are now told that the new provisions embodied in Bill No. 410 conform with the provisions of GATT. I should like to know why we have had to wait seven long years since GATT came into effect before this step is taken to strengthen the amended provisions of section 35. The weakening of section 35 was carried out in 1948 and we have waited now for seven years before the government moves to put back a little of the strength into that section that was abstracted from it in 1948.
There is one final matter which I put in the form of a question. As I have suggested, we indicated our view in 1953 that the legislation now embodied in subsection 6 of section 35 would not be adequate for the purpose. Here is abundant proof, after another year and a half of delay, that our contention was correct and that it has been fully justified. Why does not the government admit frankly the error of a year and a half ago? I ask the minister to say, now that it has been found that the legislation was unsatisfactory in its form and effect and in the powers it gave to the government, why it has taken them so long to find that their legislation was unsatisfactory for this purpose.
We are dealing with something of considerable importance. I wish to emphasize again
Customs Act
that no one has suggested that the house should follow a course not in keeping with the general agreement on tariffs and trade. It should not be necessary to make that statement, but in view of the way in which the house was invited to distort things that were said by members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition in the debate in December, 1953, it apparently is necessary to make that statement.
We are now being asked to move in the direction of strengthening and clarifying the provisions of the Customs Act. Why have we waited so long? How much harm has been done in the meantime by permitting to continue on the statute books of this country legislation which was weaker than it ever needed to be even while still conforming not only with the letter but with the spirit of the general agreement on tariffs and trade?

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to talk on this bill tonight, but as the hon. member for Eglin-ton (Mr. Fleming) proceeded I began to wonder whether we were dealing with Bill No. 29 of last session. The question of tariffs is a most important and difficult one to handle, particularly in this country with our vast areas. We are a country small in numbers, but because of our great size, because of the large proportion of our export trade, trade is vital to us, and it is far more vital to western Canada than it is to eastern Canada.
At the present time this government is fighting a magnificent rearguard action in the field of international trade against the forces of trade restriction that the hon. member for Eglinton tonight is upholding as being-

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I stated in my remarks that I hoped it would not be necessary and it should not be necessary to make the particular statement which I did at that time. speechtext: That is not a question of privilege.

speechtext:
Perhaps I could be excused for misunderstanding what the hon. member said, but it seemed to me that I heard him say that the government was being prodded and pushed into introducing legislation which-perhaps this is my confusion-was in a direction different from what we would like to see in western Canada. I say that the government is fighting a rearguard action against anything that would tend to restrict our trade. I am sorry if I said anything that would conflict with what the hon. member felt he had said. I was not thinking entirely in terms of what he was saying. I was viewing this from the larger horizon of a world that would like to throw aside restrictions and trade freely, but cannot because of misunderstanding, because of international difficulties which the great trading nation to our south is trying to overcome; and it is confusing to hear debate such as we heard on Bill No. 29. It is also pretty hard to tell sometimes whether the hon. members who are speaking are in favour of or against trade.
The administration of the great nation to our south are going a long way toward trying to remove restriction and we can see from this distance the difficulty they are having. We wish them well in that fight, and the reason we do that is that it is most important to us that they win that particular fight. We have to gain time and avoid the effects of restrictions, which almost approach insanity at times, which would take us back into something like what we had in the thirties. We have to keep away from restrictions, and if we can hold the line, as the government has been doing, we will eventually win through. It will not be by criticizing them for doing the job they are doing in keeping away from going back on the tariff road that has been travelled so often in the past.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING VALUATIONS, DRAWBACK APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a word which perhaps I might not have added if it were not for the statement, to me utterly amazing and astounding, made by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver), whom I have always regarded as one of the fairest men in the house until I heard what he said tonight. That shocked me more than I can easily say, because if anything has ever been made clear it was made clear by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that the last thing we

were seeking was to restrict trade. All that this measure is doing, as has been pointed out on both sides of the house, is to try to make effective laws which are already on the statute books. But for the hon. member for Churchill to describe the government action as fighting a rearguard action against anything that would tend to restrict trade, that to me was a fantastic statement. As the hon. member for Eglinton has said, the government has come in here seeking to strengthen legislation which it brought in a year ago last December and which at that time we suggested had certain defects-I have the book open before me.
The hon. member for Eglinton was careful to ask the question as to whether what is now proposed was in accordance with GATT, which is seeking to keep the trade lanes open, so important to us in Canada, as we all agree. It is for this reason that I rise to object most strenuously to what the member has said. I do so because there are people of the baser sort up and down this country who will seek to represent what we are doing in that very way, but I never thought to hear it from the hon. member for Churchill. I hope that he will be frank enough to admit that he was wrong and to make it perfectly clear that he now understands the situation and that it is not the fantastic one he put before us a moment or two ago.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Eglin-ton, as usual, puts everything in its worst light. There are hundreds of points of entry along the Canadian border, and that is what this refers to. Previous to this amendment, it was only required that persons should report at the nearest point of entry if they had dutiable goods. Now under the system which we have at the border points, there are many other acts which are administered there, for instance, the acts and regulations relating to immigration and health, health of animals, insect infestation and diseases of plants. I am sure that the hon. gentleman does not seriously suggest that anybody can enter this country at any place along the border and not report to somebody that he is coming into Canada.
It is in order to clarify it that this section has been put into the act. The present law requires vehicles to report only when conveying dutiable goods or when the vehicle itself is dutiable. I would suggest that modern methods of transportation are the principal reasons or one of the principal reasons why we put this into effect. If the hon. gentleman had to deal, as I do and as my administrative officers do, with all the running there is across the line with automobiles at points on back roads and bringing in smuggled goods and the like of that, he would be the first to suggest that this legislation should be changed whereby it would be an offence if these people did not report to the nearest customs point.
